Russia's 'highway to hell' logistics routes Ukraine has developed AI-enabled drones capable of making precision strikes from hundreds of kilometres away, and it means using Russia's vital logistics routes has become a dangerous "lottery".

A report last week from ACLED affirmed that Ukraine's campaign was a "drone war of attrition," with strikes against the road network carried out nearly every day since April.

"The continuation of this campaign is possible because Ukrainian forces have continuously degraded Russia's air defenses in the south," the report read.

Ms Molloy said four years into the war, Ukraine was also using technology innovations and creativity in its tactical approach.

"We see long-range capability [with drones] that traditionally could be achieved only with missiles and very expensive systems or aircraft and other weapons," she said.

"[It's] really provided the strategic edge to Ukrainian forces."

World.title: How a day at the footy built the political career of Britain's new PM
World.content:
A football tragedy when he was a teenager made Britain's new PM 'fall out of love' with politics. This is what it took to rebuild his trust and the lessons for Australia.

Grievance is having a political moment.

In Australia, a tide of voter grievance has delivered Pauline Hanson and her One Nation party to a position that threatens both the federal Coalition and Labor.

In the UK, the impact of grievance politics is being played out in even more surprising ways.

It is not just the rise of Britain's Hanson-like figure Nigel Farage, and his right-wing populist Reform movement, that has been trying to capture the grievance beast.

Grievance also explains the meteoric rise of the UK's new soft left prime minister Andy Burnham, who identifies as a socialist (albiet a moderate one). Yet in a matter of months, Burnham has catapulted from mayor of Greater Manchester to resident of 10 Downing Street.

Burnham and Farage might appear to share little in common.

One is the Labour Party outsider from Britain's north, coming to Westminster to shake up the political establishment, decades of policies of deregulation and small government.

The other is a populist who has never actually had to run anything but has risen — along with his party — to political prominence via populist policies that channel resentment towards migration and European influence over the British way of life.

Yet both Farage and Burnham have emerged at the top of Britain's political food chain because of something very similar: platforms of grievance.

The two men might define this grievance in different ways, and propose different ways of addressing it, but their messages tap something remarkably similar: resentment of "the establishment" and its perceived failure to address the concerns and needs of the average Briton.

With attempts to address this grievance now coming from Burnham on the left as well as Farage on the right, the contest in UK politics will be the great test of what modern political grievance is, and ask if — and how — politicians can truly address it.

The lessons for Australia are already significant, making this a contest that Australian voters and politicians will be watching closely.

A major left turn

Just a few weeks into his prime ministership, Burnham has leveraged voter sentiment to his benefit.

Despite considerable scepticism from the UK's powerful media, Burnham, who is Britain's seventh PM in a decade, appears to have shown an early grasp of how to turn the sense of grievance that propelled him to Downing Street into a genuine connection with voters.

Having watched our own multiple leadership changes in Australia, there are some obvious comparisons to be made.

Unlike Malcolm Turnbull, Burnham does not come to office constrained by policy pledges made to others in the party. And unlike Anthony Albanese he has not arrived constrained by attempts to paint himself as not that different to the incumbent government he was seeking to replace.

Burnham has also already proven himself better at politics, and political management, than Kevin Rudd or Tony Abbott. He represents UK Labour's first major turn left since Margaret Thatcher's conservative centre-right government in the 1980s.

The Labour PMs that followed Thatcher — Tony Blair, Gordon Brown and Keir Starmer — all identified as centre-left. The party's truly left-wing leaders of recent decades — from Michael Foot in the 1980s to Jeremy Corbyn, who led the party from 2015 until 2020 — never made it to Number 10.

Burnham, whose political views sit in the political middle of his Labour forebears, likes to paint a political picture that suggests golden days before Thatcher became Britain's first female prime minister in May 1979. But the reality is the years before Thatcher were ones of decline and strife in the UK. And the years of James Callaghan's Labour leadership that preceded Thatcher weren't actually that golden. Change was desperately needed.

The months leading up to the election that brought Thatcher to power featured rolling strikes and high inflation, an era that became known as the Winter of Discontent.

From football tragedy to political calling

If you haven't been too invested in Andy Burnham's rise to power after he contested the Makerfield by-election on July 17, you may have just picked up something about "Manchester".

But Burnham was a Westminister veteran of some 15 years standing from 2001 and 2017 before spending most of the past decade as the very popular mayor of Greater Manchester.

You may also have picked up some scepticism about whether running one of Britain's biggest cities gave Burnham sufficient training to become PM.

Burnham outlined his story, and his "vision" for transforming British politics, in the book he published in 2024 with Steve Rotheram, who has held two consecutive mayoral positions in of one of England's other great northern cities, Liverpool, since 2008. Their book, Head North, is pitched as a "rallying cry for a more equal Britain".

Their story also helps explain the foundations of Burnham's political views.

Burnham and Rotheram were born three miles, and nine years, apart on Merseyside, on the outskirts of Liverpool.

Burnham's Catholic family was considered lower middle-class, as the British classify themselves. His father worked for British Telecom as a technician and engineer. His mother was a medical receptionist. He describes a loving childhood defined by an absence of luxuries.

Burnham received a state school education and he and his older brother were the first in their family to attend university. He won a scholarship to Cambridge University to study English and has described feeling like an "imposter", shifting from working class Liverpool to this elite and privileged environment.

Burnham was working as culture secretary for then-UK Labour prime minister Gordon Brown when he met Rotheram, who was already serving as Liverpool's lord mayor.

Twenty years earlier, on April 15, 1989, when Burnham was 19 and Rotheram was 27, the two young men each went to watch the soccer. It is a sport that is woven deeply into the Liverpool community, with team allegiance held passionately, and passed down through generations.

Burnham, a lifelong Everton fan, went to watch his team play the FA Cup semi-final at Villa Park in Birmingham, against Norwich City.

A little further east, Rotheram was in the crowd watching the "other" FA Cup semi between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest at the Hillsborough Stadium in Sheffield.

What neither knew was that the match at Hillsborough Stadium that day would become the scene of tragedy: a crush of fans left 97 people dead and 766 injured when around 2,000 spectators were funnelled into a tunnel that led into an already overcrowded bay. Rotheram saw the catastrophe unfold. Some of Burnham's mates witnessed it.

Two decades later, at a service to commemorate the 20th anniversary of Hillsborough in 2009, the significance of the tragedy was crystallised into the Andy Burnham political story when he addressed 24,000 heckling football fans as part of his job representing Prime Minister Gordon Brown.

Just what had happened at Hillsborough had remained a contentious issue throughout those 20 years.

The police, media and other authorities blamed the disaster on Liverpool football fans, suggesting the crush was a result of them being late, of not having tickets and of being drunk.

An initial official inquiry carried out in 1990 cleared fans of wrongdoing and blamed the tragedy on police failures and poor stadium design. But the verdict labelled the Hillsborough deaths "accidental".

Victims' families campaigned for decades for the "accidental death" finding from the original inquest to be quashed.

Experiencing the grief and passion of grieving families at that anniversary gathering focused Burnham's mind on what he saw as the injustice and inequity of modern Britain.

Both Burnham and Rotheram describe what happened at Hillsborough as a cover-up. It underpinned in both men a political will to confront perceptions of injustice in the UK. Their proposals to change the way the UK works was outlined in their 2024 book.

"I had experienced the way our political system fails people in a very personal way and, from 2009, the realisation grew that it could only be fixed with wholesale change," Burnham wrote. "The spell was broken and I had fallen out of love with Westminster."

It led him, from his position within the Cabinet, to push in 2012 for an independent inquiry into the disaster. The inquiry was followed by a new inquest.

In 2016, the new inquest instigated by Burnham's pressure four years earlier was handed down. It ruled the victims had been unlawfully killed due to police gross negligence and operational failures.

It had been a long fight. It also defined the platform Burnham has used to craft his political brand.

He describes Britain as "one of the most politically centralised and economically unbalanced countries in the developed world".

Along with Rotheram, the now-PM offers a sobering conclusion about the nation he now leads: "We can see evidence of a country that doesn't work for most people all around us."

"Raw sewage in our rivers and on our beaches," the pair wrote. "Chaos on our railways. Energy bills beyond the means of ordinary people. Infrastructure that doesn't work for anyone. Injustices left standing for decades."

'Fixing the buses'

Burnham's policy agenda is often simplified. He is described as attempting to achieve on a national scale what he did in Manchester: a strategy simplified as "fixing the buses".

He became famous for creating Manchester's Bee Network that overturned Thatcher-era deregulation and privatisation of bus networks. Instead, Burnham delivered to Manchester a system that saw a region outside London regain control of its buses for the first time in almost four decades.

Burnham's earlier, and substantial career as a 15-year veteran of Westminster, saw him serve both in government and opposition. He entered parliament in 200, and held relatively senior cabinet positions from treasury to health, before leaving government in 2017 to become mayor.

While Burnham might come to the prime ministership with the air of an outsider, he knows how Westminster works. More importantly, from his perspective, he knows why it doesn't.

Within days of becoming PM, Burnham had made announcements aimed at acknowledging the cost-of-living pressures people were feeling.

He also tried to signal that his Labour government wanted to support the things that British people hold dear. Like pubs.

The reaction from the UK press was swift.

"All froth, no beer," read a headline from The Telegraph, suggesting Burnham's policies were weak and short sighted.

Others inferred Burnham was being patronising, pigeonholing pubs as working-class.

Meanwhile, answers to the big, macro-economic issues like tax, government debt and the defence budget are yet to be tackled.

But Burnham has proved adroit at understanding and capitalising on the speed of the modern political news cycle as well as social media.

His early measures were signals rather than comprehensive policies: a cut to tax on electricity bills and on the taxation of pubs; a cap on bus fares; and a promise to end rough sleeping.

"I'm not pretending we've solved Britain's problems. Far from it," Burnham said on social media at the end of his first week.

"But this week is a reminder that the government can make people's lives that little bit easier. That politics can work for the people. And that we don't have to settle for what others say is and isn't possible."

A manifesto for Britain's future

The manifesto that Burnham and Rotheram laid out in 2024 includes greater regional power and the return of utilities like water and electricity to public ownership, but also changes to the health and education systems alongside profound constitutional reform.

In his first speech as prime minister on July 17, Burnham promised "good growth in every postcode", saying his victory in the Makerfield by-election, which returned him to Westminster, was a call "on behalf of forgotten places everywhere up and down this country, for a return of the Labour they once knew".

"We must recognise that this generation of politicians — myself included — have failed to challenge a political culture and an economic model that simply doesn't work well enough for ordinary people."

Burnham charts that failure to "a series of wrong-turns in the 1980s".

"Four decades of the neoliberalism that began in the 1980s have not been kind to the places that built our party, nor to the communities across the UK in rural and coastal areas," he said.

"Political power was centralised and economic power was privatised.

"The country surrendered control of the essentials — housing, water, energy, transport — and left people exposed to higher costs.

"That, in turn, led to the concentration of more wealth and power in the hands of fewer people and fewer places."

Language like "nationalisation" of industries has conjured up the mass nationalisation of industry undertaken by the post-war Atlee government which extended as far as banking and heavy industry.

In reality, Burnham's targets are much more limited — starting with Britain's largest water authority, the massive Thames Water behemoth which is serving about a quarter of the country's population.

Burnham explicitly said during the Makerfield by-election that public ownership of Thames Water — privatised by the Thatcher government in the 1980s — "is absolutely an option".

Count Binface in the political mix

It is striking how much of the broader economic agenda that Burnham now pursues echoes that of Reform.

Beyond the attention always given to the movement's anti-immigration and anti-Brexit positions, Nigel Farage also talks about everyday Britons being "betrayed" by an out of touch "establishment".

Only the labels are different.

Farage blames the "progressives" in that "establishment" for causing decaying public services and economic stagnation because of their compliance with "international" rules.

Farage also advocates a move of critical utilities to more public ownership, as well as a restructuring of Westminster. In Reform's case, by the abolition of the House of Lords.

How will Burnham's government impact Reform's agenda?

Burnham's arrival on the scene may put Farage under pressure to address more hip-pocket concerns than simply relying on anti-immigrant and anti-Europe sentiment, particularly since so many Britons have had second thoughts about Brexit.

Burnham's grievance agenda has much clearer overtones of class and the long-standing north/south divide than that of Farage.

While the sorts of measures Burnham announced during his first week in office may have been small, and could even be seen as virtue signalling, they were more explicitly directed at people's everyday lives than those of Reform.

"For too many families, life has become a constant calculation," Burnham said after he took on the job. "Can we afford to put the heating on? Can we make that journey into town? Can we stretch things to the end of the month?"

That was the way he framed those early moves — cutting energy taxes, capping public transport fares to give families "a bit of breathing space".

"It's the first step in taking some of that pressure off people's shoulders," he said. "It's about giving people a moment to lift their head up and look forward again. It's a start. But I know it's only that."

Based on poll ratings, it is Farage's Reform, rather than the Conservatives, which is the most serious opponent of Burnham's Labour.

For now, Farage faces his own challenges.

He made what now looks to be a very bad call by resigning to recontest his seat — widely viewed as a cynical move to avoid an investigation into £5 million in undeclared gifts from a tech billionaire and undeclared benefits arranged by a convicted fraudster — Farage attempted to reframe it as an attempt to pitch himself as the "battler" against the "establishment".

But there has been an immediate impact in the polls.

Reform's national vote share has slipped from as high as the low-30s to the mid-20s.

The by-election for his seat of Clacton, to be decided on August 13, has descended into farce.

Farage's main challenger is a comedian who dresses as an intergalactic hero called Count Binface.

Opportunities for Farage and Reform to pursue a serious policy agenda have disappeared, at least until the by-election is over.

Moving on from grievance

Meanwhile, Burnham has announced a "listening tour" around the country this month. He is expected to visit places that have been hit hard by the closure of local industry and discuss regional energy policies.

The Conservatives, who have been notably absent from this story, concentrated much of their early attack on Burnham on his lack of foreign policy experience.

The pressures on the UK defence budget alone make that a real issue that has to be addressed, and one of immediate interest to Australia given our commitment to the joint AUKUS project.

But these pressures can wait.

As the new prime minister's strategy to tackle grievance politics takes shape, Burnham's biggest battle for now will be domestic.

And for Australian politics — and particularly Australian Labor — Burnham's embrace and shaping of his own grievance agenda raises questions about Labor's own political strategy. A strategy formed in the days when it didn't want to look too different to an incumbent government, rather than one seeking to define its very own clear mandate.

Credits

Words: Laura Tingle

Illustrations: Shakira Wilson

Editing: Catherine Taylor

World.title: The 19 questions asked in Australia's first complete census
World.content:
When you sit down to fill in the census form this week, you will be taking part in an ancient tradition.

For almost as long as human civilisation has existed, governments have counted populations.

When leaders have sought to allocate resources, structure elections or establish military forces, censuses have often been held.

From the ancient Byzantines to Australia's first national census, here's a quick history of how and why humans are drawn to count themselves.

The first counts

The first known census was taken by the Babylonians almost 6,000 years ago in approximately 3800 BC.

The records, believed to be carried out every six or seven years, were taken down on clay tablets. They counted the number of people and livestock, as well as food stores in the city.

"For the purpose of ascertaining the country's wealth, an accurate survey and census was made, and was perfected about 2500 BC," Sir George Handley Knibbs, Australia's first Commonwealth Statistician, wrote in his 1911 Statistician's Report.

Early censuses in Greece and Israel focused on counting people for military service, and, in ancient Egypt, to assess the labour force available for monument construction.

Do as the Romans do

They may not have been the first to do it, but the ancient Romans pioneered a system more like the one we use today.

Centuries before famous leaders and statesmen such as Julius Caesar, Mark Antony and Cicero walked the earth, Rome was ruled by kings.

Under that system commoners had no voting rights and were subject to unfair military burdens and taxes.

Rome's sixth king, Servius Tullius, is known for enacting sweeping social and military reforms. (Wikimedia Commons: Servius by Rouille, Guillaume Rouille, PDM 1.0)

That was until Servius Tullius, the sixth king of Rome, came to power in the 6th century BC.

He is credited with reforms that gave more people rights, which was made possible by the introduction of the census.

Ancient sources say he ordered all Roman men to register their names, ages, their family members' names, the monetary value of their properties and what district they lived in.

Using that information, Servius could assign able-bodied men to military units, establish fairer tax obligations for each household, and expand voting rights.

Ancient Roman historian Livy wrote that the census was "a most useful thing" that enabled "the burdens of war and peace to be borne not indiscriminately … but in proportion to a man's wealth".

Ancient historians offer different suggestions of the penalty for failing to register in the census under Servius, ranging from property seizure, being sold into slavery, and suffering the death penalty. Later Romans risked losing their voting rights.

A census-taking scene on the frieze of the Altar of Domitius Ahenobarbus, created in the late 2nd century BC. (Wikimedia Commons: Altar Domitius Ahenobarbus Louvre n1, Jastrow, PDM 1.0)

Romans continued to hold censuses every five years, even as the kingdom transitioned to a republic, and later, an empire.

According to Catholic tradition, Mary and Joseph were travelling to Bethlehem for a census ordered by Emperor Caesar Augustus, the adopted son of Julius Caesar, when Jesus was born.

Australia's first complete census

Australia's first population count, called a "muster", was held in Sydney Cove in 1788 and used to estimate the amounts of food and supplies needed to support the new colony.

It would not be until 1881 that an attempt to count the population of Australia in a single day was made, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders were excluded from that number for almost a century.

In 1967, Australians voted to amend the Constitution, with changes including the removal of section 127:

In reckoning the numbers of people of the Commonwealth, or of a State or other part of the Commonwealth, aboriginal natives shall not be counted.

A copy of a "personal card" supplied during the 1911 Australian census. (Supplied: Australian Bureau of Statistics)

According to the National Museum of Australia, this section of the Constitution did not prevent First Nations people from being counted in the census, but it meant they were excluded from the national population.

Earlier censuses had not accurately counted the First Nations population due to the specific phrasing of questions and the remote locations of many communities.

The 1971 census was the first to include Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders in the total population count.

The first nationally coordinated Australian census took place on the night of April 2, 1911, and asked several questions still used today.

Australia's "total population" was counted as 4,455,005. That was an increase of 681,204 people from the 1901 census.

What questions were on the 1911 census?

Here are the questions as they appeared in Australia's first complete census.

World.title: 'People are still dying': Lasting scars of Australia's tainted blood scandal
World.content:
In 1990 Tristan Stanley's parents received a chilling phone call. Their 10-year-old son, they were told, had tested positive for hepatitis C.

"My parents were in shock. They didn't know a lot about hepatitis C. They weren't even aware we'd been tested for it," Tristan tells Australian Story as he looks over his medical records.

Tristan, pictured with his parents Victor and Sandra, was infected with hepatitis C when he was about six. (Supplied: Tristan Stanley)

Following the hospital's advice, the family packed up their lives in the small town of Whyalla and moved to Adelaide so Tristan could be monitored regularly.

Having been born with haemophilia, a genetic disorder where a person's blood does not clot properly, Tristan was no stranger to hospital visits. But now, things were different.

There was anger mixed with fear. The blood product he had been given to save his life, might now potentially end it.

Tristan Stanley pictured as a little boy in the 1980s. (Supplied: Tristan Stanley)

Decades on, Tristan is determined to piece together what happened. He is one of thousands of Australians who were transfused with contaminated blood in the 1980s.

"We were told we had one of the safest blood supplies in the world. But if that's the case, how did so many get infected?" Tristan asks.

Like many who have trodden this path before him, he has received expressions of empathy from the institutions involved, but no action.

He hopes new documents he has recently uncovered will get their attention: cabinet minutes that raise troubling questions about decisions made at the peak of the crisis.

Now they might listen. Now they might act.

Loading...

A global infected blood scandal

Up to 20,000 Australians were infected with hepatitis C or HIV during the 1970s to 1990s from contaminated plasma products and routine blood transfusions.

Hundreds died, while others have lived for decades with serious medical consequences.

Infected blood was a global scandal. While countries like Canada, Ireland and the United Kingdom have had independent inquiries and established wide-ranging compensation schemes, survivors here argue Australia is yet to fully reckon with this dark chapter.

A vigil is held in London in May 2024 for the tens of thousands of UK victims of the infected blood scandal. (Getty Images: Jack Taylor)

A 2004 Senate inquiry into hepatitis C went for four days and found financial compensation was "not in the best interests" of those infected, and that best practice was followed at the time.

The findings were distressing for those who had been infected with hepatitis C from contaminated blood. Equally galling was the government's failure to follow through on a recommended national apology.

The Department of Health, Disability and Ageing told Australian Story it recognised the profound and lasting impact that, "historical contaminated blood products have had on affected Australians", and that support initiatives were implemented following the 2004 Senate inquiry.

Miracle treatment 'turns out to be poison'

Prior to the 1970s, life for someone with haemophilia was fairly grim. A bump or fall usually meant a lengthy stay in hospital to administer treatment. Bleeds were excruciatingly painful and sometimes fatal.

Then along came Factor VIII — a blood-clotting product that could be injected intravenously at home.

"It was a game changer for haemophiliacs … you could live an almost normal life," Tristan says. "But for thousands of us, this product turned out to be poison."

Tristan's father Victor gives him a dose of Factor VIII in 1994. (ABC Archives: 7.30 Report)

Unlike the previous treatment, which was made from a single blood donation, Factor VIII was made by pooling thousands of donations. It only took one infected donor to contaminate the whole batch.

Having hepatitis C meant that Tristan was constantly tired and lacked energy. Then there was the mental torment — the rumours that went around school, the questions from concerned parents.

"It took me decades to clear the virus. I went through multiple treatment options … some of them had horrible side effects."

Despite all of this, he considers himself lucky compared to his friends Tony and Niel.

Niel Lake, Tristan Stanley and Tony David were all infected with hepatitis C from bad blood. Armed with new evidence, they are pushing for answers. (Australian Story: Greg Nelson)

Like Tristan, Tony David's blood-clotting product was infected with hepatitis C.

Tony was wasting away waiting for his third liver transplant. (Supplied: Tony David)

In 2002, a 25-year-old Tony was riding high after becoming the first Australian to win the World Darts Championship. But then his liver began to fail.

Within a few years, he was on the operating table undergoing his first liver transplant. "I was absolutely shocked. I was terrified I was going to die," he says.

After a few months, the virus began to attack his new liver. He ended up back on the operating table a decade later, undergoing a second transplant. However, within weeks the second liver began to fail.

As his health rapidly deteriorated, an emaciated Tony was told he was once again dying. He underwent a third and final transplant in 2020.

"This is my last shot. If this one fails … there's not enough connective tissue to attach another liver."

Tony David in hospital during each of his three liver transplants. (Supplied: Tony David)

'I felt like a leper'

But it wasn't just people with haemophilia who were affected.

Niel Lake's health and career were ruined by hepatitis C, contracted from a post-operative blood transfusion.

"I was constantly feeling sick. I'd be sitting in my office and vomit in a plastic bag. I'd tie it up and try and get rid of it," Niel tells Australian Story.

A rising star in the Australian Federal Police, Niel was forced to take early retirement in his 30s.

Niel Lake was given a blood transfusion, which was contaminated with hepatitis C, following surgery. (Australian Story: Greg Nelson)

There was also a lot of stigma that came with hepatitis C — a virus traditionally associated with drug addicts.

"It certainly alienated me from a lot of my colleagues and friends," he says.

It also strained his personal relationships.

"I felt like a leper in my own household," he says.

After undergoing two rounds of treatment to clear the virus, which was as debilitating as the virus itself, Niel no longer has hepatitis C, but the damage to his liver had been done.

"We're often told this is an historical issue, but what [the government] fail to realise is that people are still suffering, people are still dying," Tristan says.

Watch the Australian Story 'Bad Blood' Monday at 8pm (AEST) on ABCTV and ABC iview.

Heartbreak in the courts

Like Tristan and Tony, Lyn Hatch's son Martin, born with mild haemophilia, was infected with hepatitis C. But his blood products were also carrying a more immediately deadly virus.

"To tell a 14-year-old that he's got AIDS … it was just horrendous," Lyn recalls. "But he was a brave boy until the end."

Martin Hatch died from AIDS in December 1989, aged 16. (Supplied: Sydney Morning Herald)

Martin's legal case was the first to run in Australia. Lyn would go to the courts in the morning, before heading to the hospital.

"They had a cast of thousands," Lyn says of the defendants.

"Our barristers … acted pro bono."

The findings were brought down on the day of Martin's funeral. The hospital, the Red Cross and Commonwealth Serum Laboratories were all cleared of negligence.

Lyn Hatch is still dealing with the loss of her son to AIDS from tainted blood. (Australian Story)

Apart from the emotional devastation, the family also faced financial ruin. Upon learning of Martin's HIV status, their business partner left.

"We lost our business. Our house was tied up with the business; we had to sell the house. So we ended up with nothing."

In the end, the family received $30,000 from the Commonwealth government via the Mark Fitzpatrick Trust, a limited fund set up to provide financial support for people with medically acquired HIV. Lawyers told Lyn the modest amount was due to the fact Martin was a minor with no earning capacity or dependents.

"Our family, we were worth something because of the suffering," Lyn says.

"But Martin's life actually wasn't worth anything."

Red Cross under pressure over donor screening

Lawyer Peter Gordon ran the first successful HIV case and subsequent litigation for HIV sufferers around Australia in the early 1990s.

Much of the argument focused on the Red Cross, which at the time was a state-based organisation funded by the state and federal governments.

"They knew at least by 1982 that HIV was bloodborne … and there were risk groups that should be excluded from being donors because they were more likely to be carrying the virus," Gordon says.

"People who shared needles, people who went to tattoo parlours and gay men with more than one partner. And for a period there, they simply didn't do it."

"From 1981 to 1984, Australia had the highest transfusion AIDS rate per capita in the Western world," Gordon says.

Lyn Hatch, pictured in newspaper coverage at the time, says it was "horrendous" telling her 14-year-old son that he had AIDS. (Supplied: Sydney Morning Herald)

Peter Gordon's colleague, Andrew Grech, led the bulk of the hepatitis C litigation in the 1990s.

The plaintiffs argued the Red Cross had failed to exclude high-risk donor groups (such as those with high rates of IV drug use) for a certain period, and that — apart from Queensland — it had failed to introduce a type of surrogate test that could have identified donors likely to be carrying the virus.

As the test identified signs of liver inflammation in a donor, rather than the hepatitis C virus specifically (that test wouldn't be invented until 1990), the Red Cross argued it would have led to false positives and a lot of good blood being thrown out, putting the blood supply in danger.

While a Senate inquiry would later back the Red Cross's decision, Grech maintains that by the mid-to-late 1980s, "it was known in the medical and scientific literature that hepatitis C was a significant problem" and that the test should have been introduced.

Unlike the UK, Australia has not held an independent inquiry into the infected blood scandal. (ABC News: Maisie Cohen)

The Red Cross never admitted liability, nor did the Commonwealth Serum Laboratories (which at the time was government-owned, not a publicly listed company).

However, the lawyers say they were able to establish enough of a liability case against both that the federal and state governments were forced to come to the table and settle. Together, Gordon and Grech secured compensation for about 1,000 people.

Lifeblood, formerly the Red Cross, told Australian Story: "While these events led to significant changes in blood banking in Australia and around the world, we cannot forget the harm they caused."

"Today, Australia has one of the safest blood supplies in the world, through rigorous donor screening and blood testing."

Haemophilia community locked out of hep C compensation

Australia's haemophilia community was devastated by contaminated blood. Most were infected — more than 400 died from HIV — and a further 1,350 were exposed to hepatitis C.

Of those 1,350, the majority have been unable to access existing state compensation schemes because they cannot identify the exact donor that infected them.

"The way our products were manufactured made them a higher risk of infection. They pooled thousands of donations," Tristan Stanley says.

"So, to be told you're not eligible for compensation, it's a kick in the guts."

The haemophilia community was not eligible for hepatitis C compensation schemes. (AP: Frank Augstein/Pool)

The Haemophilia Foundation of Australia told Australian Story they have been advocating for decades for a dedicated financial scheme and proposed a new scheme to the current government a year ago. The discussions are ongoing.

For hepatitis C information, support and testing contact the national HepLink on 1800 437 222.



'Facilities would be closed down': Contamination concerns

For Tristan, Niel, Tony and Lyn, the desire for compensation is not what drives them. It's their feeling that successive governments have refused to acknowledge or apologise for certain failures that took place.

"My medical records show I was treated with old high-risk product 10 months after it was withdrawn," Tristan says.

"We also have evidence of people not being told of their diagnosis, putting them at risk of infecting others."

Tristan Stanley has uncovered government documents that raise troubling questions. (Australian Story: Lincoln Rothall)

Tristan's requests to meet with the federal health minister have been declined. But he's hoping the documents he uncovered in the National Archives of Australia will not be ignored.

The 1985 cabinet minutes detail an urgent need to upgrade the Commonwealth Serum Laboratories' blood fractionation facility at Parkville, Victoria, where his blood-clotting products were made.

The facility had a world-class reputation. But the cabinet minutes tell a different story.

The document says:

"If the Department enforced the Commonwealth's own Code of Good Manufacturing Practice the facilities would be closed down immediately as not one area of the facilities complies with the Code." "Failure to upgrade could have grave political implications for the government and the department in the light of current concern about contamination of blood and blood products."

The document further details:

"… some recent batches of Factor VIII used by haemophiliacs have failed to reach the appropriate sterility standards." "Ever-increasing fears are held by all those who are aware of the state of the facilities that it is only a question of time before there are increasingly frequent and serious occurrences of producing blood factors that are contaminated with diseases such as hepatitis B and AIDS."

The cabinet minutes revealed some recent batches of Factor VIII "failed to reach the appropriate sterility standards". (Australian Story)

Tristan also obtained 1988 cabinet minutes that revealed that three years on, there were still "major problems with the existing blood fractionation plant", and that it still "fails to meet current standards of Good Manufacturing Practice by a wide margin".

"It shows the government was clearly aware of some serious issues at Commonwealth Serum Laboratories," Tristan says.

" It makes me question if safety was a priority. "

In 1994, CSL Limited was privatised and its new owners were indemnified by the government against any claims arising from contaminated blood products prior to sale.

The Department of Health did not respond to Australian Story's questions about the cabinet documents.

'Unfinished business': UK inquiry brings hope

In 2024, the UK's Infected Blood Inquiry delivered a damning report after five years of extensive hearings. It found many of the infections in the UK during the 1970s–1990s were preventable and established a broad-brush compensation scheme.

Tristan, pictured with his partner Candice, says the UK's Infected Blood inquiry reinvigorated his drive to find answers. (Australian Story: Lincoln Rothall)

For Tristan and his fellow survivors, it reignited their hope that justice was still possible.

After taking advice from a key lawyer involved in the UK inquiry, Tristan, together with Tony and Niel, headed to Canberra last month to present their case to politicians.

Having received expressions of support from members of each major political party, Tristan is feeling hopeful and determined.

"There's unfinished business. I'll keep fighting for as long as it takes," he says.

Watch the Australian Story 'Bad Blood' Monday at 8pm (AEST) on ABCTV and ABC iview.

World.title: After a big defeat, US pro-Israel lobby sets sights on midterms
World.content:
After Jamaal Bowman left his job as a New York school principal to run for Congress in 2020, he received an invitation.

The American Israel Public Affairs Committee, better known as AIPAC, wanted him to attend a meeting.

Bowman was wary of the lobby group, whose stated mission is "keeping Congress pro-Israel". He turned down the invite.

"Even at that time, amongst progressives, we likened AIPAC to the NRA," he said, referring to the National Rifle Association, another group known for its influential role in US politics.

The refusal to meet made him an AIPAC target early, he said. He later cemented that status by becoming one of Congress's chief critics of Israel.

Jamaal Bowman was targeted by AIPAC during his 2024 primary election in New York, which he lost to a pro-Israel Democrat. (Reuters: Joy Malone)

So when he was up for re-election in the 2024 Democratic primary, AIPAC and its affiliates invested big money in an effort to unseat him.

Its political spending group, the United Democracy Project (UDP), put a record-breaking $US14.5 million into ads against him.

Notably, the ads did not focus on AIPAC's core issue.

"Zero per cent [of the ads] talked about Israel," Bowman told the ABC.

"[The ads were] like, 'Oh, Jamaal Bowman is not a real Democrat because he opposed … this one part of one bill that Biden supported', whereas their real focus and agenda is unequivocal support for Israel."

Ads funded by the AIPAC-linked United Democracy Project generally do not mention Israel. (AdImpact)

Bowman lost his seat to a pro-Israel Democrat.

Senator Bernie Sanders, who campaigned for Bowman, said at the time: "Big money buys politicians who will do their bidding, and the results are clear."

AIPAC celebrated the win, labelling Bowman an "anti-Israel extremist".

Two years later, ahead of the midterm elections for the US Congress, AIPAC is deploying the strategy again.

Avoiding the issue

AIPAC boasts about a track record of success deciding election-winners.

After the 2024 elections, the group produced a memo that said 98 per cent of AIPAC-endorsed candidates had won their races.

It noted AIPAC members had contributed more than $US53 million to candidates.

But its effort against Bowman was the first time it had directed such big money towards attack ads.

The tactic now appears to be part of the AIPAC playbook.

"AIPAC never runs ads that mention Israel," said Casey Kennedy, a co-founder of Track AIPAC, which analyses and publishes details about AIPAC and its affiliates' spending.

" The issue is not popular for them. If they tried to run that messaging, it wouldn't work. So they're going to message about everything else under the sun. "

Public opinion has been turning against Israel in the US, particularly among Democrats.

In a Pew Research poll in April, 60 per cent of Americans had an unfavourable view of Israel, up from 53 per cent a year earlier.

The figure increased to 80 per cent among Democrats and Democrat-leaning independents.

Neither AIPAC nor the UDP responded to the ABC's interview requests or written questions about their advertising or other tactics.

But a UDP spokesman recently told Inside Political Money: "We run ads on issues most voters care about."

He said other political action groups used a similar strategy but were not subject to the same scrutiny because of a "media double standard".

The Michigan test

The Democrats' contest to choose a senate candidate in Michigan this week was seen as a test of AIPAC's clout — and whether its support can be toxic.

The group and its affiliates spent more than $US30 million to back Haley Stevens, the moderate "establishment" candidate, against progressive Israel-critic Abdul El-Sayed.

Why Michigan was a crucial Democrat primary Abdul El-Sayed's victory in the Democrats' Michigan primary race could shape the party's messaging to voters and how it responds to Donald Trump ahead of November's crucial midterms.

Again, the ads funded by AIPAC and its groups did not mention Israel. Some featured a 2018 clip of former president Barack Obama praising Stevens' work for the car industry. Others highlighted El-Sayed's previous criticisms of Obama.

AIPAC's support for Stevens became one of El-Sayed's key attack lines.

He described the spend on Stevens's campaign as a "$30 million down payment on a vote to send $3 billion somewhere else", referring to the US's annual military financing package for Israel.

A local poll highlighted the risk AIPAC's support could backfire in the state, which has the US's highest proportion of Arab Americans.

Democratic primary voters in Michigan were asked: Would you be more or less likely to vote for a candidate that was supported by AIPAC, or does the issue make no difference to you?

Some 40.6 per cent of voters said they would be less likely, compared to just 3 per cent who said they would be more likely, and 47.1 per cent who said no difference.

In the Democrats' senate primary race in Michigan, AIPAC-linked advertising focused on Haley Stevens's domestic policy record.

El-Sayed narrowly defeated Stevens in what was seen as a big loss for AIPAC.

But its spending still appears to be paying off elsewhere. AIPAC says 30 pro-Israel candidates won other primary elections this week.

Contentious tactics

Illinois proved another interesting case study on AIPAC's strategies during the state's primary elections earlier this year.

Forty-six Democrats competed for the party's nomination in four key seats around Chicago.

At least some of those candidates had meetings with AIPAC. One of them, state senator Willie Preston, later said AIPAC was "looking for slaves".

Public radio station WBEZ surveyed the 46 candidates in late February.

By that point, AIPAC had chosen a candidate to back in each seat.

In the survey, almost all candidates agreed that there should be strict conditions on aid to Israel, and that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. But the four AIPAC-backed candidates would not give "yes" or "no" answers, WBEZ reported.

AIPAC and its affiliates spent millions supporting those candidates. In the end, two of the four AIPAC-backed candidates won their races.

Trump's 'Mini-Mamdani' crackdown Democratic socialism is on the rise in the US, and it is sparking a sharp campaign from Republicans.

Other candidates said AIPAC-linked funding had been disguised and deceptively spent. Much of the money went through "shell" organisations, which had names like Elect Chicago Women and Affordable Chicago Now, and did not promote their ties to AIPAC.

"It [AIPAC] makes sure to wrap that money in a feel-good name and hope voters don't notice," candidate Kat Abughazaleh, one of AIPAC's targets in the Chicago races, told her online followers.

The tactic is legal but "cowardly", Track AIPAC's Casey Kennedy told the ABC.

"These groups are doing the most that they can to provide the least transparency," he said.

"This is a symptom of our very flawed campaign finance system that we have here in the US."

Unwanted support

Unusually, another AIPAC-linked group spent money in the Chicago campaign supporting a staunch critic of Israel.

A shell group called Chicago Progressive Partnership ran ads to boost progressive candidate Bushra Amiwala. She called it a "cheap attempt to smear my name".

Amiwala was not a frontrunner in her race. But Abughazaleh, a prominent local influencer who had used her platforms to criticise AIPAC and Israel, was.

So some candidates saw the move as a calculated attempt to split the anti-Israel vote to damage Abughazaleh's chances.

Abughazaleh was narrowly beaten by Daniel Biss, the mayor of a Chicago suburb.

After Kat Abughazaleh lost her primary race by a few thousand votes, AIPAC said it was "very proud to help defeat her". (Reuters: Jim Vondruska)

Biss is Jewish and his mother is Israeli, but he was not AIPAC's favoured candidate. He later wrote a piece for The Nation about his strategy to overcome the group's efforts to influence elections.

"AIPAC works so hard to hide its activities because it knows its extreme agenda is toxic to Democratic voters," he wrote.

"My strategy to beat all this back started with my confidence that if voters understood what AIPAC was doing, they would recoil.

"I made sure voters knew three things: who was funding my opponent (AIPAC and Trump donors), why they were doing so (to get a representative who would vote for no-strings-attached military aid to Israel), and how hard AIPAC was working to conceal it."

Harder to track

Overall, AIPAC says it has backed 215 winners in the US's primary elections so far.

"While disappointed that some of our AIPAC-backed candidates did not prevail, our community is proud to support pro-Israel Democrats and Republicans who stand for our values," it said in a statement this week.

The successful candidates will now represent the major parties in the midterm elections on November 3, when voters will elect 435 House members and 35 senators.

AIPAC says it will "keep working to help elect pro-Israel leaders and to help defeat anti-Israel detractors between now and November".

"We are encouraged that voters in races across this primary season continue to broadly choose leaders who support a strong US-Israel partnership," it said.

"These results demonstrate that AIPAC's nearly 7 million members remain determined to make the case for a strong US-Israel relationship that makes America stronger."

Kennedy predicts the group will do a "lot more spending" as the midterms get closer. He expects a larger proportion to go towards supporting Republicans.

But he says AIPAC-linked money is becoming more difficult to track.

One reason is because its members can donate to candidates through online portals that have been set up to prevent donors' identities becoming public.

"It's definitely getting harder, and that's intentional, and that's a reaction to the work that we're doing," he said.

"Every dollar that we report, we can account for, but it's probably an under-count to say the least."

World.title: ‘We couldn’t get over that’: The AFLW norm baffling this Irish import
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Erone Fitzpatrick is a star – All-Australian, Carlton leader and selected in the Irish representative AFLW side – but there’s one thing about Australian rules football that leaves her baffled. Club loyalty – or rather, the lack of it. Hailing from County Laois in Ireland, Fitzpatrick helped lead them to their first Gaelic football title in over 20 years in 2022, before being poached by Carlton for the 2023 season. Carlton’s Erone Fitzpatrick will represent her homeland in the ALFW Aus vs Ireland clash. Joe Armao She played with the same teammates from age four to 23; switching clubs or counties is “unheard of at home”. “Talking to a lot of the Aussies here, they can’t get over how loyal you are to your club and your county throughout your whole career,” Fitzpatrick said. “I would play with the one club for my whole football career, and I would play with the one county for my whole football career, and they couldn’t get over that.



“That’s why we find it really strange, the whole trade period and people leaving clubs and going to different clubs and stuff like that.” Fitzpatrick hopes she can stick with her AFLW side in a similar way. “I would love that,” she said. “You never know what can happen in the future, but I think it would be very weird for me to go anywhere else. I think if you asked a lot of the Irish players, they would say the exact same thing.” Since the AFLW’s inaugural season in 2017, the presence of Gaelic football cross-coders has skyrocketed, with 44 active Irish players in the league and two inactive. Their effect has been profound. The Irish players play a lightning-fast and attacking style. North Melbourne, who have won two consecutive AFLW premierships, currently have five Irish players on their list, while the Brisbane Lions, Adelaide, Geelong and Carlton all have a strong contingent of Irish players. Erone Fitzpatrick is one of 46 Irish players in the AFLW. Joe Armao The impact in Ireland has been seismic as well. On one hand, the game’s popularity has surged, with Irish broadcasters showing AFLW games, dedicated 3am watch parties and growing fan bases on social media.



But the amount of Irish-born players lured to Australia has also left a growing hole in Gaelic football pathways, especially in smaller regions, “I’m from a very small county, not saying that I would have been a big fish, but I probably would have been at home,” Fitzpatrick explains. “For my county to lose like someone like me is hard ... because in a small county, talent is very limited compared to the bigger counties that have a huge pool of talent. “Counties like Mayo have six girls playing in the AFLW – that’s a huge chunk of unbelievable talent from one county.” There’s enough Irish talent in AFLW to make a representative game in the mould of State of Origin possible. Fitzpatrick represented Ireland in that match in Sydney, in front of a sellout crowd. Speaking in the lead-up, Fitzpatrick was thrilled to be part of it. Carlton star Erone Fitzpatrick was a pivotal part of the Blue’s surge into the prelim finals. AFL Photos



“My parents are flying out for the game, which is so important to me, and I’ll also have my aunties, family friends, my grannies’ next door neighbour,” she joked. “I want to make them proud, and I want to make all the young girls proud and know they can chase their dreams and be anything they want in life.” Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 ‘Faceless’ foes to face off as Carlton and St Kilda scrap for wildcard spot Now, the focus is on the upcoming AFLW season, which begins on Sunday at Marvel Stadium when Fitzpatrick’s Blues take on the Saints before the clubs’ men’s teams do the same. The Blues’ women’s side made it to a preliminary final last season, where they fell short against the Lions. It was a meteoric turnaround – Carlton finished 14th in 2024 before introducing a crop of young, extroverted talent in 2025. Fitzpatrick was a pivotal part of the resurgence last year, averaging 17.5 disposals and kicking 13 goals.

World.title: ‘They hid it away’: The DNA test that revealed an Australian cricketer’s family secret
World.content:
But the true significance of Gaunt’s debut has been shrouded in a family secret for decades, only recently confirmed by DNA testing: Ron Gaunt may well have been Australia’s first Test cricketer of Indigenous heritage.

After moving to Victoria, Gaunt also made his mark in the east, notably as the longtime bowling coach for the Footscray Cricket Club. It was there he set Merv Hughes on the path to a storied career by telling the young all-rounder from Werribee that he was, in fact, a bowler.

“He was quick and used to swing the ball about quite nicely. Especially on the Perth wicket where he used to get a bit of pace and bounce, he was a nasty proposition for a batsman to face. He was certainly a top-rate fast bowler,” Craig told Cricinfo in 2012.

Gaunt’s story was a good one, of a strapping quick bowler with a shock of red hair, who may well have played many more games for Australia had he not been stuck behind the likes of Alan Davidson and Graham McKenzie.

Within a few days, the 23-year-old Gaunt made his debut in Durban, claiming figures of 2-87 in a drawn match under the captaincy of Ian Craig.

In January 1958, a young West Australian fast bowler by the name of Ron Gaunt was flown into South Africa as an injury replacement for the Australian Test team.

Because of its rich wheat farming, York was home to plenty of prosperous families, who shared the land with the Indigenous community.

The municipality of York, about 100 kilometres east of Perth, is WA’s oldest inland town, established in 1831 after being home to the Ballardong Noongar people for thousands of years.

Gaunt’s story also raises a wider question of Australian cricket, and life. How many more gifted athletes of Indigenous heritage have been part of the nation’s story in secret, because of the past strictures of the White Australia policy?

Since then, Ash Gardner, Scott Boland and Brendan Doggett have joined the list of Indigenous Test cricketers. Boland will proudly take the field for Australia in a Test against Bangladesh in Darwin , amidst one of the nation’s largest Indigenous communities, this week.

His debut came a month earlier than the sole women’s Test played by Aunty Faith Thomas at Melbourne’s Junction Oval in February 1958, and decades before Jason Gillespie took the field for Australia in Sydney in 1996.

As the years went by, rumours circulated that the swarthy complexion of some children was down to Spanish ancestry, or even that someone in the family had married a Pacific Island princess. Anything but Indigenous heritage.

The secrecy started around the time of the First World War, when two family members served, including Arthur Gaunt. When he came back from Europe, Arthur listed his mother’s heritage as Maori, the better to receive a gratitude bond of £100 for returned servicemen.

“All this was kept a secret,” says Ron’s nephew, Dudley Gaunt. “There were laws and restrictions, and it just would’ve made their lives difficult. So they hid it away.”

Walter and Matilda raised her eldest son, Arthur, together, but also had other children, including another named Walter. After Walter junior grew up, he married Ruby Morse, and among six children Ron Gaunt was born in York in 1934.

Matilda Gaunt, who was Indigenous, is seated at right. She was Ron Gaunt’s grandmother.

Matilda was, by all accounts, a formidable figure. Local newspaper reports tell of how, aged 16, she took the local publican to court in York over unpaid wages and won the case. She was a landowner, and after having one child with another man, Matilda married Walter Gaunt, a local bricklayer.

In 1872, John Walkinshaw Cowan, whose brother would marry the revered social reformer and politician Edith Cowan, had a child with an unnamed Aboriginal woman. That child, Matilda Cowan, was Ron Gaunt’s grandmother.

“WA was a very harsh place for Aboriginal people,” says Ron’s niece, Jenny Ewell. “I think they wanted to avoid that, and absolutely because of Ron’s cricket.

It is ironic that two of Gaunt’s three Tests were played against Apartheid South African teams – just another reminder of the complexities facing a young man of mixed race in Australia in the 1950s and ’60s.

Gaunt was among the most promising young fast bowlers in the country, with enough of a competitive streak to indulge in a bit of “Bodyline” bowling for WA in 1956. In a game against Queensland, umpire Colley ordered WA captain Ken Meuleman to change the field, and warned Gaunt about his bowling.

When the Gaunt family moved from York to Perth, as Walter’s building business grew, he purchased land and built a house in a suburb called Rivervale, on the eastern bank of the Swan River. Tellingly, Rivervale was the nearest suburb on the outside of the prohibited area, which was only rescinded in 1954 – well after Ron had started playing club cricket.

In the west, a strict policy was introduced in 1927 to ban the Indigenous community from setting foot into the “Native Prohibited Area” that broadly covered the Perth central business district and select suburbs either side of the Swan River. And in Queensland, an Aboriginal fast bowler named Eddie Gilbert was swift enough to knock the bat out of Don Bradman’s hands, but not to play for Australia.

Much had changed in WA, and Australia, between the late 19th century and the 1930s. Intermarriage between whites and Aboriginal people was first discouraged, then virtually outlawed.

Gaunt, by this time nicknamed “Pappy”, would also mentor Tony Dodemaide, and was instrumental in helping the club win its inaugural first-grade premiership in 1980.

“What he did for me was extraordinary. Without him, I would’ve gone down to Footscray and battled away as a middle-order batsman and part-time bowler. If I had said to Ron, ‘You’re kidding yourself, I’m a batsman’, I’d probably still be plugging away in Footscray thirds now...”

“I reckon I bowled three balls and Ron came down and said you don’t bat any more, you’re a bowler. He stood at the top of my mark for two or three years, just talking bowling, theories, sorting batsmen out, a whole gamut of different things.

“I was a middle-order batsman who bowled maybe second or third change and then got down to Footscray and had a talk to the president, the coach, Ken Eastwood was in on the conversation as seconds captain, and Ron Gaunt was there,” Hughes says.

“Ron absolutely loved playing cricket, he lived and breathed the game, and I think it would have just destroyed him had he not been able to play it. So that’s probably where it came from.”

Hughes remembers Gaunt’s skill as a technical coach, plus his ability to still send down beautiful outswing in the nets. But what sticks with him is the older man’s personal touch – sports psychology before it had the name.

“You could talk to him about anything,” Hughes says. “He could pick up on if you were having a bad day or whatever, and that’s the philosophy I take with kids now. You talk to them, and it’s not just about cricket, but about school, are exams coming up? If guys aren’t concentrating on their bowling, you try to get to the bottom of it, and he used to do that beautifully.

”He knew you had the talent and if you weren’t producing at training he’d try to get to the bottom of it. He’d say, ‘Listen, you’re at training, you can leave that behind, and concentrate on your training’.”

Merv Hughes was mentored by Ron Gaunt at Footscray. Getty

Some earthier incentives came when Hughes and Footscray were fighting for their lives in the 1980 first-grade grand final.

“In the first XI grand final I played in my second year at Footscray, there was 10 and 11 batting, and he just said, ‘Right boys, if you can get to double figures here I’ll buy you a slab’,” Hughes remembers. “How hard do you reckon we worked to get those runs?

“If you did well, he was always there for you. It wasn’t him beating his chest, it was just him patting you on the back and saying, ’Well done’.”

Dodemaide, a couple of years younger than Hughes, can recall watching Gaunt bowl, perhaps planting a seed that led an initially front-on bowler to change his action to allow for the away swingers that netted Dodemaide 10 Test caps.

Australian selector Tony Dodemaide (right). Getty Images

“He had the tracksuit on and was clearly well past playing age, but he went in to bowl a few balls and demonstrate what he was talking about, and he had this beautiful side-on jump and action, and it was just so smooth,” says Dodemaide, now an Australian selector. “I thought, ‘Wow, could I ever bowl like this bloke?’

“Having a couple of Test players around the club was just gold for a young kid like me. He only played a handful of Tests, but that was enough as far as we were concerned – to spend any time around someone who’d played at that level of cricket.”

None of Hughes, Dodemaide or even his fellow Footscray Test cricketer Ken Eastwoood had any idea about Gaunt’s heritage.

“I never knew that, but that’s a real feather in his cap,” Hughes says. “Times have changed for the better. I thought I spent a fair bit of time with him, but it was never mentioned. Back then he might’ve been hiding that heritage.”

There is one former teammate, Lindsay James, who has told Dodemaide that Gaunt did indeed know of his Indigenous heritage, and that the pair discussed it quietly, once, long after both had finished playing and coaching.

“I couldn’t imagine him being a fearsome fast bowler,” Dodemaide says. “He had such a gentle demeanour about him, and very generous with his time and experience.”

After retirement, Gaunt moved to the NSW Central Coast to share more time with his children, Karon and Andrew. Gaunt and their mother had divorced when Andrew was two years old.

“Once a year we used to get to see my father around Christmas time for a month, [and] then he’d have to go back to Victoria to work,” Andrew says. “But when I was around 21-22, I went and stayed with him for a few years, and that was good. He was pretty much just like a mate, he spoke like a mate and that’s how we were.

“I came back to Sydney after a couple of years, and we kept in closer contact, and, eventually, he retired up the Central Coast and I went up and stayed there for a while. But work was back here in Sydney. So I was always going up there weekly, pretty much for years.”

Australian Test players Ron Gaunt (left) who played his first Test against South Africa with captain Bob Simpson and Richie Benaud. "The News" and "The Mail"

Sport in general, and cricket in particular, was never far away from the conversation.

“You had no choice on the TV, it was cricket when it started until it finished, then he’d go, ‘OK it’s yours now’,” Andrew recalls. “He never boasted, he never bragged, that wasn’t him. Other people who knew him would say, ‘That’s Ronnie Gaunt, he used to play for Australia’. But he’d never say that. He wouldn’t talk too much about it – what happens on tour stays on tour almost.”

If Gaunt was taciturn about his cricket achievements, his heritage was buried deeper still, remaining unknown to the family when Ron died in 2012. Eight years later, during COVID-19, Andrew’s half-sister Kellie started digging into family history. Ancestry searches were followed by DNA tests, revealing a hidden Indigenous bloodline.

Indigenous Test star Scott Boland. Getty Images

“One day, out of the blue she gave me a call and said, ‘Andrew, guess what, you’ll never believe it’, and I just said, ‘Nah, get out of here’. And my other sister Karon couldn’t believe it at all.

“Then Kellie got in contact with Jenny, and she took it up and ran with it. It was a such a well-kept secret, and maybe that was a reason why. He may not have played for Australia or got the chances he did if they knew he had Indigenous background.

“I was speaking to my sisters about Jason Gillespie saying, ‘Geez, he’s supposed to be the first person of Indigenous blood to play for Australia’. I started laughing about that and going, ‘Oh man, sorry about that’.”

Ask Andrew what he might have said to his father had he known, and he pauses.

“I’d probably have said, ‘What the hell were you thinking?’” he laughs. “I’m actually quite proud or glad, it just cements that footprint in our family as a full-on Aussie. But I don’t think they looked at it like that.”

While Ron got his mother Ruby’s red hair, Andrew and Jenny are both darker in complexion. Andrew can remember, as a teenager, that Ron got them together at Martin Place in Sydney.

“I met Jenny one time when I was about 16,” he says. “Dad was in Melbourne at the time, but he came up to see us. He wanted me to go and meet my cousin, he goes, ‘Come and meet your cousin’, and Karon said, ‘What about me?’ and he says, ‘Nah, just Andrew’. I thought that was a bit odd.

“That’s the first and last time I met Jenny [who moved to the United States, where she still lives]. But I think Dad was sizing me up with her because we were both darker in complexion. That’s just my take, but my sisters Karon and Kellie thought that made sense.”

After Jenny took up the family research, she passed much of the information onto Dudley Gaunt, who still lives in WA. He has had inconclusive discussions with WA Cricket about Ron’s Indigenous heritage, and has also made attempts to contact the Ballardong Noongar community. Cricket Australia is looking into the Gaunt family story.

“We want to ensure cricket’s heritage fully reflects all those from different backgrounds who have contributed to the game,” a CA spokesman said.

“The stories provided by those exploring family ancestry is an important way to ensure the diverse backgrounds of past players is recognised.”

Dudley says the main issue in his meeting with WA Cricket was not Gaunt’s Aboriginality, “It was whether he accepted his Aboriginality, whether he told people. Did he tell people at South Perth cricket club?

“If he wouldn’t have been able to play cricket, why would he tell anyone at South Perth that he was Aboriginal? It was a different time, they parked it away, hid it and got on with their lives.”

In 2005, the former chief justice of NSW, James Spiegelman, spoke about hidden Aboriginal histories in that year’s Charles Perkins Oration.

“Let me state one undeniable fact: many, probably millions of Australians have an Aboriginal ancestor,” he said. “This should be recognised as an important bond. However, most do not know this fact about their family.

“There was a strong sense of racism involved in the suppression in thousands upon thousands of Australian families of the Aboriginal origins of one or more of their forebears. For most of our history this has been regarded as a matter to be suppressed.

“It appears to me that the process of reconciliation would be advanced by a wider recognition across the broad Australian community that the number of Australians who have Aboriginal ancestors probably amounts to millions.

“The reconciliation process cannot succeed if it is based, contrary to historical fact, solely on maintaining a rigid and categorical distinction between black and white. It will succeed if a significant proportion of those Australians of whom it is true take pride in acknowledging their roots in both communities.”

For Jenny, the secret is itself a significant part of the story.

“I was very proud to find that out myself, to think we’ve got heritage that goes back 60,000 years in Australia,” she says. “But in going back to speak to the family, I found out that the family did know, and didn’t say anything.

“I was shocked, thinking, ‘Gosh they kept it a good secret all those years’. But a lot of it might have been that they wanted to work and get on with their lives. This is my opinion – because Ron was playing cricket and very successful, they wanted that to keep going and that it wasn’t made more difficult for him.”

Andrew recalls one other comment from his father that has taken on new meaning.

“My dad used to tell me, ‘You have a whole other family in the west’,” he says. “It was a big secret, and back then I could understand it. Whereas now I’m like, ‘Wow, that’s cool’.”

World.title: How an Australian mining company was caught in Trump’s tightening Cuba noose
World.content:
Exclusive WorldNorth AmericaForeign relations How an Australian mining company was caught in Trump’s tightening Cuba noose Michael Koziol August 9, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On the outskirts of a city called Moa, at the south-eastern end of Cuba, flies a Canadian flag. Its maple leaf flaps proudly beside the red triangle and white star of Cuba’s own national banner. The flags mark the Moa Nickel mine, a joint venture between Canadian mining company Sherritt International and Cuban state-owned La Compania General de Niquel. Ore is extracted, shipped to Alberta in Canada and refined into nickel and cobalt. The Canadian flag flies next to the Cuban flag at the Moa Joint Venture, a nickel mine in southeastern Cuba. Google Maps In May, as part of efforts to crush Cuba’s communist regime, the Trump administration imposed sanctions on Moa Nickel. The mine, already hit by fuel shortages after the US choked off Cuba’s Venezuelan lifeline, has shut down – as has Sherritt’s refinery in Fort Saskatchewan, Canada. Now, the Trump administration is doing the same thing to a fledgling gold and copper mine part-owned by an Australian company, Antilles Gold. And in both cases, the solution appears to be the same: sell a stake to the Americans, possibly to friends of US President Donald Trump.



“Their choices are to leave, stay and then have an immense amount of problems, or try to find a saviour,” said John Kavulich, president of the US-Cuba Trade and Economic Council, a New York-based business network. “If I’m an executive of Antilles Gold in Australia, I’m waiting for someone to stick a gun in my stomach. Thus far, that’s the only thing the Trump administration hasn’t done.” ASX-listed Antilles Gold was slapped with US sanctions in early June when its Cuban joint venture, Minera La Victoria, was blacklisted. The company, which is headquartered at an unassuming home in the NSW town of Bowral, owns 50 per cent of the venture through its Cayman Islands-registered subsidiary, Antilles Gold Inc. Its main project is the Nueva Sabana open-pit copper and gold mine in central Cuba, 25 kilometres south-east of Ciego De Avila. According to Antilles’ ASX filings, the earthworks, water supply and site preparation began in early December, and a Chinese company, Xinhua Mining, was given the go-ahead on a $US30 million ($42 million) engineering and construction contract on New Year’s Eve.



Antilles Gold says work has halted while it scrambles to deal with the impact of June’s sanctions. It says the company has submitted a proposal to the US State Department that would involve selling at least 51 per cent of shares in the Caymans-based subsidiary to an acceptable US investor. Who might that be? The company’s chairman, Brian Johnson, won’t say. Neither will Kavulich, who has been working with Antilles Gold. “I can’t go there,” he said. The Moa Nickel mine in Cuba, a joint venture between Canada’s Sherritt International and a state-owned enterprise. Google In the case of Canada’s Sherritt International, its potential saviour is an entity called Gillon Capital – the family office of Heather and Ray Washburne, who happens to be a close ally of Trump. The companies are in exclusive negotiations for Gillon to take a 55 per cent stake in Sherritt at a discount to its closing value on May 15 (it had already crashed from $US0.25 a share to $US0.09 following the US sanctions).



The State Department and US Treasury cleared the way for the talks to take place, but will need to approve any final deal. Washburne is a businessman, investor and real estate developer who co-founded a restaurant chain in Texas. A long-time Republican donor, in 2016 he was described by the Texas Tribune as “Trump’s most visible fundraiser is Dallas”. Ray Washburne, pictured in 2018, was a major fundraiser for Donald Trump in Texas, and was appointed by him to run the Overseas Private Investment Corporation. Getty Images for Concordia Summit In his first term, Trump appointed Washburne to run the Overseas Private Investment Corporation, the federal government’s development bank, and he later served on Trump’s intelligence advisory board. He no longer holds either position. Sherritt’s initial response to the expanded US sanctions was to say it would relinquish its stake in the Cuban venture, which it built over 30 years. But that changed. Bloomberg News reported that Sherritt’s interim chief executive, Peter Hancock, was at home in Canada watching cycling when Washburne called him to make the offer.



“This deal happened because an actor in the United States was able to make a case to the US State Department,” Hancock told Bloomberg. “We were collateral damage in a larger policy objective for the United States.” Washburne doesn’t see it that way at all. Reached by phone on Thursday (US time), he said he was rescuing Sherritt and its mine from certain ruin, and the Trump administration had nothing to do with arranging the deal. US President Donald Trump boards Air Force One on Friday. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson “The company was in severe financial straits to begin. I’ve known about the company for years, I’ve followed it, I knew that it had some valuable assets to it,” he told this masthead. “When I saw the sanctions were put in place – I didn’t have any idea they were doing that – I just called the company and said: do you need capital? If I hadn’t come in, it would have already been shut down and gone.”



Gillon Capital was spun out of an existing family office, A. G. Hill Partners, linked to the Hunt family dynasty. Washburne’s wife Heather, née Hill, is a descendant of Texas oil tycoon Haroldson Lafayette Hunt Jr, who secured the rights over much of the enormous East Texas Oil Field. Related Article Explainer

Trump diplomacy ‘Cuba is finished’: What does Trump want with the island nation? Gillon does not own any other mining interests at present, although the family – through oil heirs Nelson and William Hunt – once owned part of one of the world’s largest silver mines, in Idaho. Washburne says he cold-called Sherritt himself when he saw the Canadian miner was in trouble. “I literally just found the guy’s phone number … It had nothing to do at all with the administration. I had no discussion with them at all.” He said he was not aware of Australian company Antilles Gold and its Cuba venture, and was not in discussions with them. But he was interested, and asked for their contact details. Washburne’s late mother was Australian, born in Sydney between the wars.



Antilles Gold chairman Johnson told this masthead that the company had identified a suitable American investor, and it was not Gillon Capital, although he would not disclose who it was. The firm’s proposal to the State Department remained confidential, he said. The Australian government confirmed it had engaged with Antilles Gold and US officials on the matter, but would not answer questions about those discussions. The State Department did not respond to inquiries. Cuba’s former president Raul Castro, 94, arrives at a gathering for International Workers’ Day in Havana on May 1, 2026. AP John Kirk, a professor emeritus of Latin American studies at Dalhousie University in Nova Scotia, Canada, said it was noteworthy that the State Department appeared to have no objection to Gillon Capital taking over the mine in Cuba. “Clearly, Trump is supporting his friends in the stealthy takeover of Cuban commerce,” Kirk said. “I suspect that a similar path will be found for Antilles Gold. In both cases, greed, hypocrisy and bullying have been implemented by the Trump administration.”



ASIC records show Antilles Gold was first registered in South Australia in 1984 as Aytox Pty Ltd. It has been through several name changes; as EnviroGold and Panterra Gold, it developed a mine in the Dominican Republic in the 2010s. The company had been turning its attention to a second Cuban project, a planned gold, silver and antimony mine on the Isla de la Juventud (the Isle of Youth). Infill drilling was supposed to start at the La Demajagua mining concession in the second half of this year, until the sanctions hit. A man pulls a cart carrying drinking water during a power outage in Havana, Cuba, last week. AP Photo/Ramon Espinosa For foreign firms, the main effect of US sanctions is on banking. Any company using US dollars is likely to be cut off by a financial institution. Even if there’s doubt, banks are generally risk-averse and won’t want to take the chance, Kavulich says. The US continues to impose new sanctions on Cuba and its interests. On Thursday, it designated a number of entities and people related to the procurement and sustainment of Cuban weapons.



“They went after the Cuban companies and ministries that everyone knows about first,” Kavulich says. “Now, they’re going granular, and they’re going deeper and deeper and deeper.” Related Article Updated

Cuba US brings criminal charges against former Cuban president Raul Castro Asked whether he thought the Trump administration’s approach to foreign companies operating in Cuba was effectively a shakedown, he said: “One person’s shakedown is another person’s benevolent opportunity to do what’s right.” Last month, the State Department released a 100-page report on the dangers Cuban communism posed to America and the Western world.
